content: Geographic tongue, also referred to as benign migratory glossitis, erythema migrans, or continental tongue, is a condition that affects the tongue. The name geographic tongue is derived from the map-like appearance of the affected areas on the tongue. The upper surface of the tongue is normally covered with small projections called papillae. In individuals with geographic tongue, there are red patches on the tongue's surface that are surrounded by grayish-white borders. These red areas lack papillae, while the grayish-white borders have an overcrowding of papillae. The patches can disappear and reappear within hours or days, and they may change in shape or size. Although the condition is typically painless, some individuals may experience a burning or stinging sensation, particularly after consuming certain foods such as spicy or citrus foods. Chemicals, including mouthwashes and teeth whiteners, can also exacerbate the condition. In some cases, geographic tongue may cause numbness, and it is often observed alongside fissures on the tongue. Histopathologically, geographic tongue is characterized by irregular areas of dekeratinized and desquamated filiform papillae, which appear red in color. These areas are surrounded by elevated whitish or yellowish margins due to acantholysis and hyperkeratosis. Neutrophils infiltrate the epithelial layer, forming structures known as Munro's abscesses. The exact cause of geographic tongue remains uncertain. However, it tends to run in families and is associated with several genetic factors. The condition is more commonly observed in individuals with environmental sensitivities, such as allergies, eczema, and asthma. Some researchers suggest that stress or diets high in sugar and processed foods may also play a role. Geographic tongue affects approximately 6% of Americans, 4% of young Iraqis, and 2% of young Finns. It is more prevalent in females, who are affected three times more often than males. Diagnosis of geographic tongue is typically made through physical examination, with the characteristic appearance of the tongue being a key diagnostic feature. There is no known cure or universally prescribed treatment for geographic tongue. However, certain measures can help manage the condition. Avoiding foods that trigger symptoms, such as spicy or acidic foods, may provide relief. Some individuals report temporary improvement after taking Vitamin B supplements. Burning sensations may also be alleviated with the use of antihistamines. The condition is generally asymptomatic, and persistent, significant pain is rare. Geographic tongue is not associated with any known systemic diseases. Recent findings suggest that the condition may respond to oral zinc supplementation, such as Solvazinc®, raising questions about whether it is caused by an allergy or a nutritional deficiency.
